title: Digital Marketing in Ticino: A Guide for Businesses
description: Bellinzona, Locarno, Lugano and the Mendrisiotto work differently. What changes for your campaigns, for the border and for how you write.
og_description: The canton holds different economies and a border that shifts the catchment: what changes for the campaigns of a business in Ticino.
h1: Digital Marketing in Ticino: Four Markets, Not One
hero_alt: The sun setting over the sea
intro: Setting a campaign to cover the whole of Ticino looks like the obvious choice: it is a small canton, you can cross it in a little over an hour. In practice it means putting the same budget on economies that have little in common, and asking one message to work for all of them.

This guide starts there: what separates the areas of the canton, what changes if you have clients or suppliers across the border, and why, with few enquiries and slow decisions, it pays to think in terms of a path rather than a single campaign.

p: Bellinzona is an administrative city, built around services and public employment. The Locarno area lives largely on tourism, with a pronounced season. Lugano is the hub for services and finance. The Mendrisiotto, down towards Chiasso, is the industrial and logistics side, and the one most closely woven into Italy.

That is four different typical clients, with different problems and different good months. An ad written for a hotel owner in Ascona does not speak to a Bellinzona fiduciario, the Swiss name for the professional who keeps a company's books, and neither of them recognises language written for a logistics company in Stabio.
The useful move is not to split the budget four ways, but to choose: which of these economies holds your best clients, and start there with a message that looks like it.

In the Mendrisiotto and all along the border strip the real catchment does not end at customs. Part of the customer base arrives from Como and Varese, and part of the workforce crosses the border every morning. Businesses selling to the public know this already; businesses selling to other businesses often underrate it.

There are two concrete consequences. The first is that the geographic area of a campaign should be set by looking at where clients come from, not by where the administrative border runs. The second is that the message has to hold up in two contexts: someone reading from Italy and someone reading from Switzerland do not have the same expectations about prices, timings and guarantees.
If that flow matters to you, say so explicitly on the site. Writing that you also serve clients arriving from Italy heads off some of the questions and qualifies others.

sections.h2: Writing in Italian Isn't Enough: You Have to Write for Switzerland
p: The Italian of Ticino is Italian, but the references are not. Prices are in francs. The rules that count are Swiss. And part of the professional vocabulary is different: a fiduciario is not the commercialista of Italy, and the reader notices on the first line.

Copy that takes the Italian context for granted communicates one thing only, which is that it was not written for the person reading it. In a market where trust builds slowly, that is an expensive start.

The check takes a few minutes: reread the text asking whether a company in Bellinzona would recognise it as addressed to them. Currency, legal references, public holidays, the names of the professions.

sections.h2: Few Enquiries and Long Cycles: You Need a Path, Not a Campaign
p: In a canton this size the number of possible enquiries in a month is limited, and in many sectors the decision takes weeks or months. A campaign judged on the number of enquiries it generates measures the wrong thing, and pushes you to spend more filling a funnel that does not have that problem.

What you need is a path: collect the few enquiries there are, work out straight away which of them are real, and stay present for the ones that will decide later on. At these volumes the difference between closing and not closing is usually the follow up, not the first contact.
In practice that is three things: qualify every enquiry by talking to it, keep track of who said not now, and have something to send those people in the months afterwards that is not a chaser.

A client in Bellinzona reaches Lugano in half an hour, and that changes the realistic radius of a business. The catchment does not stop at the municipality, and it is almost always wider than it looks to someone setting it from the map of their own town.

It works in both directions: you can serve more areas than you are considering, and your competitors are not only the ones with a sign on your street. Before tightening the radius of a campaign, look at where the clients you already have come from.

Lined up: choose the economy of the canton you are speaking to, rewrite the main pages so they are recognisable to someone reading from Switzerland, set the geographic area from real client data instead of from the border, and only then work out how much to spend on advertising.
If you work mainly in the city, the guide to Lugano gives a sharper picture: the city market has rules of its own, and they are not those of the rest of the canton.

We work remotely, with our operations base in Durrës, and we look after businesses in Italy, Switzerland, the rest of Europe and the United States. We have no offices in Switzerland. Every enquiry is called and qualified before it reaches the client.

summary: The canton holds different economies: administrative, tourist, financial and industrial.
Along the border the real catchment runs past customs, in both directions.
Italian yes, but with Swiss references: francs, rules and the names of the professions.
With few enquiries and slow decisions, the follow up counts more than the first contact.
Short distances widen the catchment: look at where the clients you already have come from.

faq.q: Is it better to run campaigns across all of Ticino or in one area?
faq.a: Usually one area, at least to begin with. The areas of the canton have different economies, and a single message ends up speaking well to none of them. Pick the one where you already have your best clients, check that it works, and widen only after that.

faq.q: Is it worth addressing clients across the border too?
faq.a: It depends on your area and your sector. Along the border strip a real share of the customer base arrives from Como and Varese, and ignoring it means leaving out enquiries that would have come anyway. The way to check is to look at where the clients you already have come from, not to decide it in the abstract.

faq.q: What language should campaigns in Ticino be written in?
faq.a: Italian, but written for a Swiss audience: prices in francs, Swiss legal references and the local professional vocabulary. If you have clients across the border as well, consider separate versions rather than one text trying to speak to everyone.
